title: Chemical competency: reading labels and safety data sheets
audience: Cleaners, cleaning supervisors and team members in any cleaning-group business who open, dilute, apply, store or dispose of cleaning products.
learningOutcomes: Read a product label and state the hazard, dilution, protective equipment and first aid directions before first use.
Find and interpret the safety data sheet for a named product in the site record.
Dilute and apply a product to its label directions, water first, without combining it with any other product.
Store and dispose of used and unused product so that customers, colleagues and property are not exposed.
Stop work and escalate when a product has no label, no safety data sheet or unknown contents.

instruction.heading: Why chemical competency comes first
instruction.body: Chemical competency means knowing what a product does, how strong it is, what it can damage, and what happens when it meets another product. Most avoidable chemical incidents in cleaning come from three habits: mixing products to get a stronger result, using a product from a container nobody can identify, and skipping gloves for what seems a small job. Every later method in this set, including mopping, buffing, washing and washroom cleaning, depends on handling products correctly. Before you open any product, you should be able to say what it is, how it is applied, and what to do if it reaches skin or eyes.

instruction.heading: Reading the label and the safety data sheet
instruction.body: The manufacturer label is the first document to read. Check the product name, hazard warnings, directions for use and dilution, protective equipment, first aid and storage directions. The detailed document is the safety data sheet, or SDS. The source material for this lesson uses the term COSHH data sheet, which belongs to a UK framework; on Australian jobs use the term SDS. Under the national model work health and safety approach, a business keeps a hazardous chemicals register, and the register must be kept up to date and readily accessible with a current SDS for each listed chemical. State and territory regulators confirm how that position is adopted, so check your own jurisdiction. The SDS sections you will use most are hazard identification, first aid, handling and storage, and personal protection. If a label is missing, faded or torn, do not use the product.

instruction.heading: Checking the site before the first use
instruction.body: Before using any product, check the site binder or digital record for a risk assessment and an SDS for that exact product. If either is missing, stop and ask your supervisor before you use it. This rule applies even to products that look familiar, because similar bottles can hold different concentrations. Customer-supplied products are used only if the business has approved them and their SDS is on file. Confirm the approval rule in your business procedure before you accept a customer's product.

instruction.heading: Diluting and applying correctly
instruction.body: Fill the bucket with water first, then add the measured product. Adding the product first causes foaming, and a splash from a bucket that is already diluted is less concentrated than one that is not. Measure to the label and do not estimate. Never combine two products, including two products from the same range, and never add anything other than water to a dilution unless the label directs it. Replace the lid straight after use, and keep trigger sprays switched to off when they are not in use. The label check does not end when the bottle is open: read the dilution again each time you prepare a new bucket.

instruction.heading: Protective equipment, ventilation and disposal
instruction.body: Wear gloves whenever you handle a cleaning product. The source states that gloves are issued to every employee and worn at all times with chemicals. Add eye protection when the label or SDS warns of splashing, and when you are diluting a concentrate. Open windows or doors where possible so fumes disperse, and treat ventilation as part of the duty of care for your own team and the customer. Spent solution goes to a sluice or other designated disposal point. Never pour product into a kitchen sink or a toilet bowl. Dispose of unused product so that a customer, child or pet cannot reach it.

procedure: Read the label before opening the product and identify the hazard, dilution, protective equipment and first aid directions.
Find the risk assessment and the SDS for the product in the site record. If either is missing, stop and ask your supervisor.
Put on gloves, and eye protection where the label or SDS requires it.
Open windows or doors where possible before you dilute or apply the product.
Fill the bucket with water first, then add the measured product at the label dilution.
Apply the product as directed. Do not combine it with any other product.
Replace the lid or switch the trigger to off. Keep the product labelled and upright in storage.
Dispose of spent solution at the designated point, never into a kitchen sink or toilet. Record any spill or exposure.

workedExamples.situation: On a bond clean you find a spray bottle with no label, a jug of product with a torn label, and a request from the client to use their own degreaser.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which products can you use, and what do you do next?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the unlabelled bottle or the torn-label jug. Set both aside, record their location, and tell your supervisor. The client's degreaser can be used only if the business has approved it and its SDS is on file. If the approval or SDS is missing, ask before any use. A product you cannot identify is never used.

workedExamples.situation: A kitchen-cleaning job has a stubborn stain, and a colleague suggests adding a little of a second product to the bucket to make it stronger.
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse to mix. Mixing products can release harmful fumes, and the label and SDS define how each product is used. Ask the supervisor for an approved product or method for the stain. Use only the single approved product, diluted in water to its label directions.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves suitable for the product, worn at all times when handling chemicals.
Eye protection where the label or SDS warns of splash, and during dilution of concentrates.
Labelled spray bottles and containers with secure lids or triggers.
Measuring device matching the label directions.
Site binder or digital record holding risk assessments and SDS for every product on site.
Designated sluice or disposal point for spent solution.

commonErrors.error: Mixing two products to get a stronger result.
commonErrors.prevention: Use one product at its label dilution. Ask your supervisor for an approved alternative.

commonErrors.error: Adding the product to the bucket before the water.
commonErrors.prevention: Water first, then the measured product. This reduces foaming and splashback.

commonErrors.error: Using a product from an unlabelled container because it looks like the usual one.
commonErrors.prevention: Set it aside, record it and report it. Never decant product into unmarked containers.

commonErrors.error: Skipping gloves for a quick job.
commonErrors.prevention: Put gloves on before you open any product, whatever the size of the job.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Under the national model WHS approach, a business keeps a hazardous chemicals register with a current SDS for each listed chemical, readily accessible to workers. Confirm how your state or territory has adopted this position.

From 1 December 2026, the Workplace Exposure Standards list is due to be replaced by the Workplace Exposure Limits list, according to WorkSafe Victoria's hazardous substances page (date checked 2026-11-02). Check which list applies in your state or territory and any monitoring that follows from it.

The source uses the UK term COSHH. Australian workplaces use the WHS framework and the SDS. The specific PPE duties, dwell times and dilution ratios for each product come from its label and SDS, and this lesson does not set them.

Applying pesticides or other regulated substances may require a licence or authority in your state or territory. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to apply, store or transport regulated substances.

qualityStandard: Label read before first use, with hazard, dilution, PPE and first aid stated without prompting.
Safety data sheet for a named product located in the site record, and its first aid and handling sections explained.
Product diluted to the label directions, water first, with no mixing of products.
Work stopped and escalated where a label or SDS is missing or contents are unknown.
documentationEvidence: Product check record before first use, including where the SDS was found.
Record of any unlabelled or unidentified product, its location, time found and who was told.
Record of any spill, splash or exposure, with first aid given and who was informed.
summary: Read the label before you open the product.
No risk assessment or SDS means stop and ask before use.
Water first, then the measured product. Never mix two products.
Wear gloves at all times, open ventilation where possible, and dispose of spent solution at the designated point.

knowledgeChecks.question: You are about to use a cleaning product for the first time. What comes first?
options: Read the label, then find the risk assessment and safety data sheet for that product
Test it on the customer's most visible surface to see how strong it is
Mix it with your usual product so the result is stronger on the visible surface

knowledgeChecks.question: A washroom bucket is being prepared. Which order is correct?
options: Add the product first, then the water so the whole job is done sooner
Fill with water first, then add the measured product at the label dilution
Add water and a second product together, then the first product

knowledgeChecks.question: You find an unlabelled bottle that may contain a cleaner. What do you do?
options: Use a small amount to test whether it works on one surface
Pour it into a labelled bottle and use it as normal
Set it aside, do not use it, record it and tell your supervisor
